title: Chemical Reactions and Equations
strapline: Recognising a chemical change, naming its type, and writing it down.
bigIdea: A chemical reaction rearranges atoms into new substances. Every reaction can be classified, and every reaction can be written as an equation that accounts for every atom.
priorKnowledge: Unit 3: metals and non-metals, reactivity trends.
futureLearning: GCSE: balanced symbol equations with state symbols, ionic equations, reacting-mass calculations.

misconceptions.misconception: Any change that looks dramatic (bubbling, colour change) is a chemical reaction.
misconceptions.whyItSticks: Dissolving fizzy tablets and boiling both bubble.
misconceptions.addressIt: Give a sorting task with deliberately tempting physical changes; require pupils to name the new substance formed as the test.

misconceptions.misconception: Balancing an equation means changing the little numbers in the formula.
misconceptions.whyItSticks: Changing subscripts makes the numbers work, so it appears to succeed.
misconceptions.addressIt: State and enforce: formulae are facts, coefficients are choices. Use models so changing H2O to H2O2 visibly makes a different substance.

misconceptions.whyItSticks: Ash weighs far less than the log.
misconceptions.addressIt: Burn magnesium in a crucible and weigh; mass increases. Account for oxygen from the air.

misconceptions.misconception: Thermal decomposition and combustion are the same because both involve heating.
misconceptions.whyItSticks: The Bunsen is present in both.
misconceptions.addressIt: Contrast directly: combustion needs oxygen and releases energy; decomposition needs energy put in and uses no oxygen.

keyVocabulary.definition: The substances you start with / the new substances formed.
A reaction with oxygen that releases energy.
The breakdown of a compound into simpler substances using heat.
A reaction in which a substance gains oxygen.
A reaction in which a more reactive element takes the place of a less reactive one in a compound.
Reactants on the left, an arrow, products on the right, written in words.
A symbol equation with equal numbers of each type of atom on both sides.

practicals.title: Burning magnesium and measuring mass change
hazards: Intense UV light from burning magnesium
control: Never look directly at the flame; lift the lid only briefly
Allow the crucible to cool on a heatproof mat before weighing; use tongs throughout

practicals.title: Thermal decomposition of copper carbonate
hazards: Copper carbonate is harmful if swallowed
Suck-back of limewater into the hot tube
control: Remove the delivery tube from the limewater before stopping heating

practicals.title: Displacement reactions of metals and metal salts
apparatus: copper sulfate, magnesium sulfate, zinc sulfate, iron sulfate solutions
small pieces of Mg, Zn, Fe, Cu
hazards: Copper sulfate solution is harmful and an irritant
control: Goggles; wash hands after handling; use a well plate to limit quantities

formative: Balancing equation ladders with immediate self-marking.
Whiteboard drill: name the reaction type from a description.

summative.title: Chemical Reactions assessment
summative.style: 30 marks, 45 minutes, including four equations to balance and a displacement results grid to interpret.
summative.markSchemeNotes: Do not credit balanced equations achieved by altering subscripts, even where atom counts match.

lessons.title: Physical or chemical change?
objectives: Justify a classification using evidence of a new substance
retrieval: State the law of conservation of mass

sequence.detail: Five questions drawing on Units 1 and 2.
Six short stations: ice melting, iron rusting, sugar dissolving, magnesium in acid, wax melting, copper sulfate hydration. Pupils classify and state the evidence.
Formalise the test: has a new substance formed and is the change easily reversed?
Discuss the deliberately tricky cases; correct the common errors as a class.

keyQuestions: What single piece of evidence best shows a new substance has formed?
challenge: Argue the case that hydrating anhydrous copper sulfate is a chemical change despite being reversible.
lessons.homework: Classify ten household changes with justification.
lessons.exitTicket: Give the best test for a chemical change.

lessons.title: Word equations
objectives: Write word equations from descriptions of reactions
retrieval: Name the products when magnesium burns.

sequence.detail: Classification recall.
Structure of a word equation; the arrow read as 'reacts to make', never as 'equals'. Naming rules for oxides, chlorides and sulfates.
I do / we do / you do across six reactions.
Twelve word equations from prose descriptions.
Common naming errors surfaced and corrected.

keyQuestions: Why do we never write an equals sign?
What is the product called when iron reacts with sulfur?
support: Naming rules card; six of the twelve with the products supplied.
challenge: Write word equations for reactions with two products, including neutralisation.
lessons.exitTicket: Write the word equation for calcium burning in oxygen.

lessons.title: Combustion and oxidation
objectives: Describe combustion as a reaction with oxygen
Explain why mass increases when a metal burns
retrieval: Write a word equation for magnesium plus oxygen
State the law of conservation of mass.

sequence.detail: Word equation practice, three items.
Burn magnesium in a crucible; mass before and after; calculate the mass of oxygen gained.
Oxidation defined; combustion of fuels contrasted with combustion of metals; incomplete combustion mentioned as a hook to later work.
Exit ticket.

keyQuestions: Why does the mass go up when we burned it away?
Where did the extra mass come from?
support: Calculation frame for mass of oxygen gained.
challenge: Use the mass data to find the ratio of magnesium to oxygen atoms and comment on the formula MgO.
lessons.homework: Explain the mass increase when copper is heated in air.

lessons.title: Thermal decomposition
retrieval: What is the test for carbon dioxide?

sequence.detail: Four questions on combustion.
Copper carbonate heated; colour change green to black; limewater turns milky.
Thermal decomposition defined; explicit contrast table against combustion on three criteria: oxygen needed, energy in or out, number of reactants.
Word equations for the decomposition of four metal carbonates; predict products for a fifth.
Exit ticket and misconception check.

keyQuestions: Why does the limewater go milky?
Is this reaction exothermic or endothermic? How do you know?
support: Products supplied for two of the four equations.
challenge: Explain the industrial importance of decomposing calcium carbonate in cement manufacture.
lessons.homework: Compare combustion and thermal decomposition in a structured table.
lessons.exitTicket: Give one difference between combustion and thermal decomposition.

lessons.title: Displacement reactions
objectives: Predict whether a displacement reaction will occur
Explain displacement using the reactivity series
retrieval: Which is more reactive, magnesium or copper?

sequence.detail: Reaction-type naming drill.
Pupils complete a blank 4x4 prediction grid before any practical work.
Metals and metal salt solutions in a well plate; record reaction or no reaction; compare with predictions.
Deduce the reactivity order from the results grid rather than being told it.
Exit ticket.

keyQuestions: How do the results let you order the metals without being told?
Why does copper never displace anything here?
support: Prediction grid with two cells completed as worked examples.
challenge: Predict outcomes for two metals not tested, and justify from the deduced order.
lessons.homework: Six displacement word equations with predictions.
lessons.exitTicket: Will zinc displace copper from copper sulfate? Explain.

lessons.title: Balancing symbol equations
objectives: Explain why balancing is required by conservation of mass
retrieval: State the law of conservation of mass

sequence.detail: Formula reading and atom counting, four items.
Model the atom-counting table method. State the rule: never change a subscript. Model three examples of increasing difficulty.
Balancing ladder, worked together for the first three rungs.
Balancing ladder continued independently, self-marked; models available for pupils who are stuck.
Address the subscript misconception explicitly with a non-example.

keyQuestions: Why can I not just change H2O to H2O2 to balance the oxygen?
What does the big number in front actually mean?
support: Atom-counting tables pre-drawn; model kits at the bench.
challenge: Balance equations involving brackets and polyatomic ions.

lessons.title: Review and assessment
objectives: Consolidate reaction types and equation writing

sequence.detail: Reaction-type flashcards and three equations to balance.
30-mark assessment.
Self-prediction of score and weakest topic.

support: Periodic table and formula sheet permitted.
challenge: Write and balance an equation for an unfamiliar reaction from a description.
lessons.exitTicket: Which reaction type do you find hardest to identify?
